sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ebisu** ​(*ebisu*) — ‌Fishermen, ‌Commerce, Luck ​· The ​foreigner, ​straggler — ​belongs ​to the ‌Japanese tradition, ​where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Fishermen, ​Commerce, ‌Luck". The ​name ​means "The ​foreigner, straggler"[^1].

​**Ebisu** ​is the ‌most ​approachable of ‌Japan's ​fortune gods. ‌With his ​fishing ‌rod in ​one ‌hand and ​a sea ​bream ‌(*tai*) under ‌the ‌other arm, ​he smiles ​at ‌merchants, fishermen, ​and ​anyone who ‌earns a ​living ​by honest ‌work. ​He is ‌the ​only native ​Japanese member ​of ​the Seven ‌Gods ‌of Fortune ​(*Shichifukujin*).[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores ​the name ​as ‌**Ebisu** and ‌serves its ‌temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/ebisu/). ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ​a description ‌computed ​from the ​displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII ​form *ebisu* ​survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ‌not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested ​in Japanese ​characters ​as ​**恵比寿**. ​Etymologically ‌it ​means ​"The ‌foreigner, straggler"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII ​form ‌*ebisu* ​survives ​only ​because ​the early ​domain-name ‌system ​could ‌not ​carry ‌diacritics; ​it ‌is a ​technological ‌compromise, ​not ​an ‌ancient ‌spelling. ‌The ​Unicode restoration ​**Ebisu** ‌recovers ​the ​full ‌diacritic ​detail ​of ‌the scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly ​in ​the ​address ​bar. ‌The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— ​a ​description ‌computed ‌from ‌the ‌displayed form ​itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**e** ​→ ​**E** — ​Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**b** ​→ ​**b** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**i** → ​**i** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**s** ‌→ ​**s** ​— ​Same
- **u** ​→ ‌**u** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the name ​is **/e.bi.sɯ/** ​— ​Modern Standard ​Japanese ​(Hepburn).[^1]

Phoneme ‌by phoneme:

- ​**E-** ​— Close-mid ‌front ​[e]; possibly ‌from ​'ebisu' meaning ‌'stranger' or ​'foreigner'
- ​**-bi-** — ​Bilabial ​[b] plus ​close ‌front [i]
- ​**-su** — ‌Voiceless ​alveolar fricative ‌[s] ​plus close ‌back unrounded ​[ɯ]; ‌the final ​vowel ​is soft

‌For ‌the modern ‌speaker, the ​closest ​approximation is: ‌'EH-bee-soo' ​— light, ​even ‌syllables; the ​final 'u' ​is ‌barely voiced.

​Kindred ‌and historical ​forms of ​the ​name:

- **Japanese** ​— ‌恵比寿 (Ebisu), ‌one ​of the ‌Seven Gods ​of ​Fortune
- **Older ‌associations** ‌— Kotoshironushi, ‌Hiruko, ‌and foreign-sea ​figures of ‌the ​Kojiki
- **Pairing** ​— ​Benzaiten and ‌Daikokuten, fellow ​members ​of the ​Shichifukujin

‌Ebisu keeps ​its ​restoration plain: ​plain Hepburn. ‌His ​name may ‌derive ​from a ‌word ​for 'foreigner' ‌or 'straggler,' ‌reflecting ​his origins ​as ​a deity ​associated with ‌outsiders ‌and the ​sea.

sections.body:
**Ebisu** ​is ‌the most ‌approachable ​of ​Japan's ​fortune ​gods. With ​his ‌fishing ​rod ​in ‌one hand ​and ‌a ​sea ‌bream ​(*tai*) under ​the ​other ​arm, ​he ‌smiles at ​merchants, ‌fishermen, ​and ‌anyone ​who earns ‌a ​living ‌by ​honest ​work. He ‌is ‌the ‌only ​native ​Japanese member ‌of ​the ​Seven ‌Gods ​of Fortune ​(*Shichifukujin*).[^1]

### ‌Fisherman ​God

‌Patron of ​those ​who ​draw ​wealth ‌from the ‌sea, ​especially ‌fishers ​and ​seafood merchants.

### ‌God ‌of ‌Commerce

‌Protector ​of markets, ‌shops, ​and ​fair ​dealing ‌in everyday ​trade.

### ​Shichifukujin

​The ‌only ​native kami ​among ​the ‌Seven ​Gods ‌of Fortune.

### ​Sea ‌Bream

​The ‌tai ‌fish is ​auspicious ​because ​its ​name ‌puns on ‌'medetai' ​(auspicious).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Ebisu has no single ​founding myth. He grew from several older figures ‌— the castaway child Hiruko, the oracular ‌Kotoshironushi, and deities of the foreign sea ​— into the cheerful merchant god of the ​Edo period. The sources disagree about which ​ancestor is truly his; the smile, the fishing ​rod, and the sea bream are the ​tradition's own answer.[^1]

### Hiruko, the Leech Child ‌(Kojiki)

The *Kojiki* tells that when Izanagi and ​Izanami first coupled, their child Hiruko was ​born 'without bones', like a leech or a ‌premature thing; at three he could not ​yet stand. The dismayed parents set him adrift ‌in a boat of reeds and let ​the sea decide. He survived — and ‌later tradition, above all at Nishinomiya Shrine near ​Kōbe, identified the foundling with Ebisu: the ​child the gods abandoned who became the god ​of those who make their own living ​from the water. The chronicles themselves never ​call Hiruko 'Ebisu'; the identification is medieval and ‌early-modern tradition, and scholars treat it as ​a genealogy of meaning rather than a datum. ‌Its content is exact: **Ebisu is the ​outsider who prospers — the stranger, the ‌latecomer, the one the palace forgot**.[^2]

### Kotoshironushi and ​the Yielding of the Land (Kojiki)

Another ‌line of descent runs through Kotoshironushi, son of ​Ōkuninushi, the great god of the land. ‌When the heavenly grandchild's envoys demanded that ​the earth be yielded, Ōkuninushi deferred to his ​son's counsel: Kotoshironushi answered on his father's ‌behalf and then withdrew to the sea, or ‌hid his body, leaving the land to ‌the new line (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki). He was ​a god of oracles, of fishing, and ​of the boundary between the human settlement ‌and the deep water; he is still enshrined ​at Shirayama-hime in Kaga and at Miho ​in Izumo, shrines that keep exactly the oracle-and-fishing ‌profile the Ebisu cult later borrowed. Several ​shrine genealogies — and much popular etymology ​— have since folded him into Ebisu, which ‌is why the fortune god carries a ​fishing rod rather than a purse. The merger ‌makes theological sense: the god who **surrendered ​territory and kept the sea** became the ​patron of everyone who draws wealth from outside ​the city's walls.

### Ebisu the Smiling Merchant ​(Edo period)

By the Edo period the composite ‌figure had found his final form: the ‌smiling god with a fishing rod in ​one hand and a great red sea bream ‌(*tai*) under the other arm, guardian of ​shops, fish markets, and honest trade. His image ​stood by the cash box and the ‌shop curtain; his festival, Tōka Ebisu at Osaka's ‌Imamiya Ebisu Shrine (10–12 January), became one ‌of Japan's greatest commercial rites, with its ‌lucky-straw charms (*kichi-zuna*) and the red-and-white 'lucky maidens' ​(*fuku-musume*) who crowd the lanes. The sea ‌bream is itself a pun: *tai* echoes *medetai*, ​'auspicious.' In Ebisu, Japan canonized a god ​of **small prosperity honestly won** — the ​daily takings, not the treasure vault. Merchants wrote ‌his name on their ledgers and brewers ​on their casks; the god of the millionaire's ​district, Naniwa's own, had made the corner ​shop his shrine.

### The Deaf God and ‌the Treasure Ship (Folk religion)

Folk tradition supplies ​the mythic punchline to his outsider status: ​when all the kami of Japan assemble at ​Izumo in the tenth month, Ebisu — ‌who is deaf, the stories say — ​**never hears the summons and stays home**. That ‌is why the tenth month is *kannazuki*, ​'the month without gods', almost everywhere, but *kamiarizuki*, ‌'the month with gods', in the east, ​where Ebisu keeps watch alone. At New Year ‌the picture reverses: the Seven Gods of ‌Fortune sail into port on the *takarabune*, ​the treasure ship, Ebisu's rod and bream prominent ​among the cargo of rice bales and ​coral, and children sleep on a takarabune print ​in the hope of a lucky first ‌dream (*hatsuyume*). The god who missed the ‌meeting becomes, once a year, **the first guest ​of fortune to arrive**.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Ebisu ​is the ‌great combiner ‌of Japanese ​religion. His ​roots are ​the Kojiki ​figures Hiruko ​and Kotoshironushi; ‌his body ​is ​the medieval ‌cult of ​the 'foreign' ‌sea gods; ​his career ‌is pure ​Edo merchant ​culture; and ​his congregation ​is ​the imported ‌circle of ​the Shichifukujin, ‌the Seven ​Gods of ‌Fortune — ​six of ‌whom arrived ​from ‌China and ​India by ​way of ‌Buddhism, while ‌Ebisu alone ‌is native. ​He is ​conventionally paired ‌with Daikokuten ​as ​the twin ‌patrons of ​prosperity, and ​the two ‌sometimes appear ​as a ‌single double-faced ​image. In ​the medieval ​Tendai ​scheme the ‌Seven Gods ‌were read ​as protective ‌manifestations of ​the Lotus ​Sutra, Ebisu ‌included. No ‌other Japanese ‌deity ‌so neatly ​braids **indigenous ‌kami cult, ​Buddhist imports, ​and the ​everyday economics ‌of the ​town**.[^1]

Kindred ​figures ​in the ‌PuniCodex cross-tradition ​index include ​[[benzaiten|Benzaiten]] (seven ​Lucky Gods ‌/ fortune ​pair), [[inari|Inari]] ‌(japanese fortune ​and harvest ‌deities), ​[[caishen|Cáishén]] (wealth ‌/ prosperity ‌/ abundance), ​[[freyja|Freyja]] (wealth ​/ prosperity ​/ abundance), ​and [[lakshmi|Lakṣmī]] ‌(wealth / ‌prosperity / ​abundance).

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Ebisu ​is ‌everywhere ‌in ​Japanese ​commercial ​life: ​shop signs, ​menus, ‌bank ​logos, ​New ‌Year ​prints, ‌and ​the ‌great ​January ​crush ​at ​Osaka's ​Imamiya ‌Ebisu and ​Kobe's ‌Nishinomiya ​shrines. ‌The ​Yebisu ‌Beer ​brand ‌(Sapporo, ​launched ​1890) ‌took ‌both ‌its ​name ​and its ‌logo ​from ​the ‌god, ​making ​his ‌face ​one ‌of ​the ​most ​reproduced ​in ‌modern Japan. ‌Railway ​stations, ‌shopping ​districts, ​and ‌baseball ‌crowds ‌invoke ‌him; ​the ‌shopkeeper ​balancing ​the ​day's ‌ledger still ​murmurs ​'Ebisu-sama.' ​He ‌remains ​what ​the ​Edo ‌townspeople ​made ‌him: ​the ‌**patron ​of ‌the ‌ordinary miracle ​by ​which ​honest ​work ‌becomes ‌daily ​bread**.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Ebisu ​is a ‌cultic ‌and ​commercial figure ​rather ​than an ​excavated ​one; ‌his material ​record ​is the ‌vast ​folk-art ‌corpus of ​the ‌Edo and ​Meiji ​periods. ​Votive tablets ​(*ema*) ​from Osaka ‌and ​the ‌fishing ports ​of ‌the Inland ​Sea ‌show ​the rod, ‌the ​bream, and ​the ‌tall ‌court cap; ‌woodblock ​New Year ​prints ‌(*nishiki-e*) ​fixed his ​smiling ‌face in ​the ​national ‌imagination. The ​Tōka ‌Ebisu ​festival at ​Imamiya ​Ebisu Shrine ​preserves ‌the ‌full apparatus ​of ‌merchant devotion ​— ​lucky ‌straw, fuku-musume, ‌gold-leaf ‌charms — ‌as ​a ‌living tradition ​centuries ​deep. The ​Kojiki's ‌Hiruko ​narrative has ​no ​archaeological correlate; ‌the ​god's ​'evidence' is ​the ‌continuing rite ​itself, ‌performed ​each January ‌in ​the lanes ‌where ‌the ​merchants still ​set ​out their ​first ‌scales ‌of the ​year.[^1]

sections.label: Kojiki & Nihon Shoki
sections.body:
Japan's two earliest chronicles, the Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE), record Ebisu in mythic narratives of cosmogony and imperial descent. The name appears in kanji logographs whose readings were later fixed by tradition.

The restoration Ebisu preserves the romanized scholarly form derived from those classical sources.[^1]

sections.label: Shinto Sources
sections.body:
Shinto ritual texts, shrine records, and norito prayers preserve the cultic identity of Ebisu. The kami is honored at shrines associated with fishermen, and festival calendars perpetuate the name.

The Unicode form Ebisu gives that ongoing tradition a precise digital address.[^1]

sections.label: Japanese Buddhist Sources
sections.body:
Japanese Buddhist literature and art sometimes assimilate Ebisu into Buddhist cosmology, mapping kami onto dharmic protectors and bodhisattvas. The honji-suijaku discourse provides a framework for such identifications.

The restored name Ebisu appears in both Shinto and Buddhist contexts in the PuniCodex archive.[^1]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Ebisu ​teaches that ‌prosperity is ‌not ​reserved for ​the ​mighty. The ​fisherman, the ​shopkeeper, ‌the noodle-stall ​cook — ​all ‌have a ​fortune god, ‌and ​he is ‌smiling. ​In a ​religious landscape ​crowded ​with austere ​buddhas and ‌clan ​ancestors, Ebisu ‌stands for ​the ‌sanctity of ​the ‌everyday: the ​first sale ‌of ​the year, ​the catch ‌that ‌pays the ‌rent, the ​ledger ​that almost ‌balances.

​His smile ​is the ‌doctrine. ​Other gods ​demand; Ebisu ‌approves. ​His deafness ‌— the ​folk ​detail that ​explains ​why he ‌alone stayed ‌behind ​when the ‌kami went ​to ​Izumo — ‌is a ‌kind ‌of perfection: ‌he ​cannot hear ‌the summons ​to ​leave, so ​he cannot ‌leave. ​Prosperity, like ​the tide, ​is ‌always somewhere; ​the ​trick is ​to be ‌the ​god who ‌stayed to ​receive ‌it. To ​work honestly ‌and ‌smile about ​it ​is, in ​Ebisu's quiet ​theology, ‌already a ‌form of ​prayer.[^1]
